patient.chief_complaint: Prolonged unresponsiveness with eye deviation, stiff posturing — initially diagnosed as stroke, now EEG shows GPDs, team unsure if NCSE
patient.hpi: A 44-year-old Black female social worker presented to a community hospital with acute left gaze deviation, left-sided facial droop, and right-sided arm posturing. Initial NIHSS was 14. The stroke team activated and CT showed no hemorrhage, CTA showed left MCA M1 occlusion. tPA was administered and thrombectomy team was called. During the window for tPA administration, the neurology fellow noted the patient had a brief 30-second rhythmic jerking episode of the right arm that was attributed to post-ischemic cortical spreading depression. NIHSS decreased to 8 after tPA. The patient was transferred to your tertiary center for thrombectomy. On arrival, she is confused, continues with subtle right arm posturing, and has a left gaze preference. EEG was ordered because the floor team was concerned about whether right arm movements were seizure activity. An electroencephalographer notes the EEG shows 'generalized periodic discharges — could be post-tPA ischemic NCSE or metabolic changes.' The team is debating whether to treat as NCSE with benzodiazepines vs proceeding directly with thrombectomy. CRITICAL TIMING ISSUE: Every minute of continued MCA occlusion kills additional brain — thrombectomy must not be delayed, but NCSE could worsen neurological injury if untreated.

medications.frequency: IV infusion completed 45 minutes ago at outside hospital

family_history: Mother: hypertension, stroke at 62. Father: diabetes. No family history of epilepsy.

social_history.note: Social worker. Single, lives alone. Non-smoker. Rare alcohol. No illicit drugs. Poorly medication-adherent per chart notes.

eeg.impression: IIC pattern — difficult to classify as definitively ictal or interictal. RIGHT ARM POSTURING: could be post-ischemic motor activity or NCSE. Do not delay intervention to perform prolonged EEG evaluation. Clinical correlation recommended.

abnormal_values_summary: Glucose 192 (high) — worsens stroke outcomes; needs insulin protocol

findings.location: left MCA territory (insular cortex, lenticular nucleus)

ct.impression: Acute left MCA territory ischemia with hyperdense left M1 thrombus. No hemorrhagic transformation post-tPA. Large vessel occlusion confirmed — thrombectomy indicated. Early ischemic changes in insular/lenticular region (ASPECTS 7 — treatable).
recommended_actions: IMMEDIATE thrombectomy — ASPECTS 7 with LVO, good treatment candidate
Last known well: within 6-hour window — proceed
Control BP to 140-180 systolic during procedure

output.impression: LPDs resolved by 24 hours — good prognostic sign for penumbral recovery. Continue levetiracetam and monitor. Clinical correlation recommended.

Left MCA territory infarct with core infarct 40 mL. No hemorrhagic transformation. The EEG LPDs and post-reperfusion seizures arose from the ischemic penumbra and cortex adjacent to infarct core. Levetiracetam appropriate for post-stroke seizure prevention. Clinical correlation recommended.

interactions.description: No pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction between alteplase and levetiracetam. Levetiracetam does not affect fibrinolysis or coagulation.
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Levetiracetam is safe to administer concurrently with or immediately after tPA. No dose adjustment needed.

output.summary: Levetiracetam + tPA = no interaction. Safe to load levetiracetam during or immediately after tPA in acute stroke with concurrent seizures/NCSE.

results.title: Seizures and status epilepticus in acute ischemic stroke: management principles
results.key_finding: EEG changes (LPDs, GPDs) are common in large MCA strokes and represent ischemic cortical irritability. Do not delay thrombectomy for EEG evaluation or NCSE treatment. Levetiracetam IV is safe to load concurrently. Benzodiazepines should be avoided in acute stroke — lower BP, worsen cerebral perfusion. Post-stroke NCSE: treat with levetiracetam; avoid phenytoin (worsens ischemic outcomes), avoid excessive sedation.

output.summary: Acute stroke + EEG changes: thrombectomy FIRST, EEG evaluation does not supersede time-sensitive intervention. Levetiracetam safe to start. Avoid benzodiazepines in acute stroke (BP-lowering effect). Post-stroke LPDs usually resolve with reperfusion; persistent NCSE requires AED treatment.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Acute left MCA ischemic stroke with post-ischemic LPDs (ictal-interictal continuum) and post-reperfusion seizures requiring concurrent thrombectomy and levetiracetam loading

differential.key_features: Autoimmune panel negative; acute MCA LVO on CT/CTA is the primary diagnosis; LPDs are post-ischemic, not from independent epileptiform process
CTA confirms left M1 occlusion — true LVO; NIHSS 14 with positive CTA rules out Todd's paralysis; post-tPA NIHSS improvement supports true ischemic stroke treatment response
Hyperdense left M1 on CT, positive CTA — LVO confirmed; not hemiplegic migraine

optimal_actions.action: IMMEDIATE thrombectomy — left MCA M1 LVO with ASPECTS 7, within time window; do NOT delay for EEG evaluation
IV levetiracetam 1500 mg loading dose CONCURRENTLY with thrombectomy prep — safe, no interaction with tPA or thrombectomy
Do NOT give IV benzodiazepines for EEG LPDs in acute stroke — lowers BP, worsens cerebral perfusion in penumbra
EEG monitoring 20 minutes pre-procedure to document LPD pattern
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Left MCA territory LPDs on IIC — post-ischemic

optimal_actions.action: Post-thrombectomy continuous cEEG 24 hours for post-reperfusion seizure monitoring
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Early post-reperfusion seizures controlled with levetiracetam

optimal_actions.action: Treat hyperglycemia — glucose 192 in acute stroke worsens ischemic injury; insulin protocol to target 140-180 mg/dL
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Glucose controlled to 140-180 range during acute ischemia

optimal_actions.action: MRI brain DWI 24h post-thrombectomy to assess infarct core and penumbral salvage
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Core infarct 40 mL with penumbral salvage

critical_actions: Thrombectomy IMMEDIATELY — do NOT delay for EEG evaluation in acute LVO stroke
IV levetiracetam (not benzodiazepines) for concurrent post-stroke seizure management — benzodiazepines lower BP and worsen penumbral perfusion
Insulin protocol for glucose 192 — hyperglycemia worsens stroke outcomes
Post-thrombectomy cEEG 24 hours for post-reperfusion seizure monitoring
contraindicated_actions: IV benzodiazepines for EEG LPDs in acute stroke — lowers BP, reduces cerebral perfusion pressure in ischemic penumbra
Delaying thrombectomy to evaluate and treat EEG LPDs — every minute of LVO delays costs additional penumbra
Phenytoin for post-stroke seizure prevention — sodium channel blockade worsens ischemic neuronal injury
key_reasoning_points: Acute LVO stroke + EEG changes: thrombectomy takes absolute priority over seizure management — time is brain
LPDs in acute stroke are post-ischemic cortical irritability, not independent NCSE — levetiracetam is appropriate concurrent treatment without delaying thrombectomy
Benzodiazepines in acute stroke: contraindicated as BP-lowering effect reduces cerebral perfusion pressure in ischemic penumbra — levetiracetam is safe
Post-reperfusion seizures are common and expected after LVO recanalization — levetiracetam pre-loading reduces early post-stroke seizure burden
Phenytoin worsens ischemic outcomes via sodium channel blockade and local vasoconstriction — never use phenytoin for post-stroke seizures

red_herrings.data_point: EEG LPDs noted on urgent EEG — read as 'possible NCSE' by resident
red_herrings.intended_effect: Delay thrombectomy while treating presumed NCSE with benzodiazepines
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: LPDs in acute MCA stroke are post-ischemic — do not delay thrombectomy. Treat with levetiracetam concurrently, not benzodiazepines. Thrombectomy is the priority.

red_herrings.data_point: Right arm posturing every 30-60 seconds during EEG recording
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest ongoing motor NCSE requiring immediate benzodiazepine treatment
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Right arm posturing in left MCA stroke is a sign of hemispheric dysfunction (posturing from ischemia + possibly post-ischemic cortical irritability) — NOT sufficient to delay thrombectomy. Levetiracetam loading is appropriate without benzodiazepines.

metadata.teaching_points: Thrombectomy priority over EEG in acute LVO; benzodiazepines lower BP in stroke (contraindicated); levetiracetam safe in stroke; post-stroke LPDs are ischemic not independent NCSE
metadata.pitfalls: Delaying thrombectomy for EEG-confirmed NCSE treatment; giving benzodiazepines in acute stroke; treating LPDs as equivalent to NCSE requiring same intensity treatment
metadata.clinical_pearl: Acute LVO + EEG LPDs: THROMBECTOMY FIRST. Levetiracetam concurrently (not benzodiazepines — they lower BP). Post-reperfusion cEEG monitors for early seizures.
